title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
interviewAnswer: Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a specified size when it truly exists. Sample-size planning links baseline variance/rate, significance level, desired power and minimum detectable effect.
keyPoints: Power is defined relative to an alternative effect size.
Low power produces noisy, inconclusive experiments.
why: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.
intuition: Power is defined relative to an alternative effect size.
deepDive: Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a specified size when it truly exists. Sample-size planning links baseline variance/rate, significance level, desired power and minimum detectable effect. Smaller MDE requires more samples. Low power produces noisy, inconclusive experiments. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.
workedExample: Plan an A/B test to reliably detect a 1% relative conversion lift before launching it.
commonMistakes: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.
followUps: What assumptions does Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size make?
How would you validate or debug Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size in practice?
production: In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.
